explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text calls them "…the leaders of Israel, the heads of their families…" and says they were "…the tribal leaders who had supervised the registration." (Numbers 7:2). These are the men who were already counting heads, and now they come with gifts in their hands. Counting people and then bringing carts is a serious upgrade in job description.

Close, because Aaron's family does serve at the tabernacle. Aaron, the priest, had sons, and one of them, Ithamar, shows up later in this chapter (Numbers 7:8). Exodus 28:1 names Aaron's sons as Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. But the men presenting this offering are called "…the leaders of Israel, the heads of their families…" the tribal leaders who supervised the registration (Numbers 7:2). They are the givers here, not the priests.

I get why you picked it, since the Levites are all over this chapter. But they're on the receiving end. The leaders bring the gifts, and then Moses gives the carts and oxen to the Levites (Numbers 7:6). The ones presenting the offering are "…the tribal leaders who had supervised the registration." (Numbers 7:2).

explanations.answer: Six covered carts and twelve oxen
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The text says they brought "…six covered carts and twelve oxen…" (Numbers 7:3). That's an ox from each leader and a cart from every two leaders, so the math works out clean. Twelve oxen and six carts showing up at once is not a quiet delivery.

Chariots sound fancy, I know. But the text says "…six covered carts and twelve oxen…" (Numbers 7:3). Carts are for hauling, and they're about to haul things for the tabernacle work. Nobody here is racing anybody.

The number is right, but the gifts are off. The leaders brought "…six covered carts and twelve oxen…" (Numbers 7:3). No tents and no camels are in this list. They presented the carts and oxen before the tabernacle, and that's the whole gift.

explanations.answer: Accept them for the Tent's work
explanations.explanation: Right on. The LORD tells Moses, "Accept these gifts from them, that they may be used in the work of the Tent of Meeting." (Numbers 7:5). Then He says to give them to the Levites, and Moses does (Numbers 7:6). I know a lot of gifts that end up in a closet, but these ones get a job.

explanations.answer: Send them back to the leaders
explanations.explanation: Nope, no returns at this counter. The LORD says, "Accept these gifts from them…" (Numbers 7:5). Moses takes the carts and oxen and gives them to the Levites (Numbers 7:6). Nothing goes back to the leaders.

explanations.answer: Offer them on the new altar
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think so, with an altar right there. But the LORD says the gifts "…may be used in the work of the Tent of Meeting." (Numbers 7:5). Then Moses gives the carts and oxen to the Levites (Numbers 7:6). Nothing here says to offer them on the altar.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says to give the gifts to the Levites, "…to each man according to his service." (Numbers 7:5). That means no equal slices like one cookie handed to every person no matter the job. Each gets what the work calls for.

Yes, it's false. The LORD says to give the carts and oxen to the Levites, "…to each man according to his service." (Numbers 7:5). Some jobs need more carts than others, so the shares are different. Moses follows that, and the Gershonites and Merarites get different amounts (Numbers 7:7-8).

That's him, baker! The text says the Merarites' carts and oxen were "…all under the direction of Ithamar son of Aaron the priest." (Numbers 7:8). That's four carts and eight oxen to look after. Somebody had to be the one watching that herd, and I'd have lasted about five minutes before I lost count.

Good guess, since Eleazar is another son of Aaron (Exodus 28:1). But the text names a different son. It says the carts and oxen were "…all under the direction of Ithamar son of Aaron the priest." (Numbers 7:8). Mixing up two brothers is easy to do, and I once mixed up two whisks.

That's a fine name, but he isn't the one here. Phinehas is not mentioned in this passage. The text says it was "…all under the direction of Ithamar son of Aaron the priest." (Numbers 7:8). Ithamar is the one overseeing the Merarites.

explanations.answer: They carry the holy objects on their shoulders
explanations.explanation: You got it. The text says they get none "…since they were to carry on their shoulders the holy objects for which they were responsible." (Numbers 7:9). Their job was done on foot, with the holy objects on their shoulders. So a cart would not have fit the work.

explanations.answer: They camp too far from the tabernacle
explanations.explanation: That sounds reasonable, but the text gives no such reason. It says the Kohathites got none "…since they were to carry on their shoulders the holy objects for which they were responsible." (Numbers 7:9). It's about the kind of work they were given. Distance never comes up.

explanations.answer: They already have carts of their own
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but carts of their own never come up in the text. The reason it gives is that the Kohathites "…were to carry on their shoulders the holy objects for which they were responsible." (Numbers 7:9). Their job was done on their shoulders, so wheels weren't what the work called for. I once tried to carry a full tray of cookies on my head. Don't ask how that went.

Yes, day. The LORD tells Moses, "Each day one leader is to present his offering for the dedication of the altar." (Numbers 7:11). That's twelve leaders across twelve days, one per day. Everybody gets their own turn at the altar, and nobody has to fight for a spot.

A week each would stretch this out to nearly three months, and that's not what the LORD says. He says, "Each day one leader is to present his offering for the dedication of the altar." (Numbers 7:11). So it's one leader a day. Twelve leaders take twelve days.

A month each would take a full year, and that's way too slow. The LORD says, "Each day one leader is to present his offering for the dedication of the altar." (Numbers 7:11). One leader, one day, and then the next one steps up. I've had cookie batches that took longer than that, but not twelve of them.

explanations.answer: Above the mercy seat on the ark
explanations.explanation: That's right. Moses "…heard the voice speaking to him from between the two cherubim above the mercy seat on the ark of the Testimony." (Numbers 7:89). The text says, "Thus the LORD spoke to him." What a way to end the chapter.

explanations.answer: Beside the altar in the courtyard
explanations.explanation: Good thought, since the altar is the star of this chapter. But the text puts Moses inside the Tent of Meeting, and he heard the voice "…from between the two cherubim above the mercy seat on the ark of the Testimony." (Numbers 7:89). So the voice isn't in the courtyard. It's from between the cherubim above the mercy seat.

explanations.answer: Behind the curtain at the door
explanations.explanation: I can see picking a curtain, since curtains sound like a spot for a voice. But the text doesn't mention one here. It says Moses "…heard the voice speaking to him from between the two cherubim above the mercy seat on the ark of the Testimony." (Numbers 7:89). The voice comes from above the mercy seat.
